blocks.content: Imagine you’re building a food delivery app.
A user places an order, and your system needs to reserve the restaurant item, deduct the user’s wallet balance, and create the order record—all in one flow.
Now think about this: what if the wallet is charged, but the order is never created? Or the item is reserved, but the payment fails? Or the system crashes in between?
These kinds of partial failures can leave your system in a broken and inconsistent state.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024003-577259247.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of an order flow that reserves an item, deducts a wallet, then crashes before creating the order record, leaving inconsistent state

blocks.content: That’s exactly why ACID transactions exist. They make sure that critical operations like this are handled safely and reliably, so either everything completes successfully or nothing is applied at all.
ACID stands for four key properties that define a transaction:
["Atomicity → all-or-nothing execution","Consistency → data always follows rules","Isolation → transactions don’t interfere with each other","Durability → once committed, data is permanent"]
items: Isolation → transactions don’t interfere with each other

blocks.content: In this section, we’ll understand each of these properties, why they matter, and how databases ensure them internally.

Without ACID, a crash at the wrong millisecond could leave your database in a broken state money debited but never credited, inventory decremented but order never recorded. ACID is what prevents that.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282727924-788358153.png
blocks.alt: Diagram summarizing the four ACID transaction properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability

blocks.content: 1. Atomicity ( all or nothing )
A transaction is indivisible. If it has 5 operations, either all 5 succeed and get committed, or all 5 are rolled back as if they never happened. There is no "partial success."
Without atomicity: Arjun books a flight. Seat is reserved. Payment fails. Seat stays reserved but no ticket issued. Flight is now overbooked and Arjun paid nothing.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130292-996265868.png
Without Atomicity :
Here, operations are executed one by one without treating them as a single unit. First, the seat is successfully marked as “reserved.” Then, the payment step fails due to an error (like a timeout).

Since there is no rollback mechanism, the first step remains applied. This leaves the system in a broken and inconsistent statethe seat is reserved, but no payment was made. This kind of partial update can cause serious issues in real systems.
With Atomicity:
Here, both operations are wrapped inside a transaction. The system starts with BEGIN, performs the seat reservation, and then attempts the payment.
When the payment fails, the database triggers a ROLLBACK, undoing the seat reservation.
As a result, either everything succeeds or nothing is applied, keeping the system consistent. This is what atomicity guarantees no partial updates, always a clean and reliable state.

Atomicity is implemented using a write-ahead log (WAL). Every change is written to the log before being applied to the actual data. If the transaction fails, the DB replays the log in reverse to undo the changes.
2. Consistency ( valid state to valid state )
blocks.text: 2. Consistency ( valid state to valid state )

blocks.content: A transaction can only bring the database from one valid state to another. It can never violate the rules you've defined constraints, foreign keys, check conditions, triggers. The DB rejects any transaction that would break those rules.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130292-918894753.png
blocks.alt: Consistency  valid state to valid state

blocks.content: With Consistency :
The system ensures that all rules are followed during the transaction. Initially, A has 100 and B has 0. When A sends 50, both steps (debit A and credit B) are completed correctly.
So A becomes 50 and B becomes 50. The total money remains the same (100), and all constraints are satisfied. The database ends in a valid and correct state.
Without Consistency:
Here, the system does not enforce rules properly. A sends 50, so A becomes 50, but B is not updated and remains 0.
Now the total money becomes 50 instead of 100, which violates the system’s rules. This leads to an invalid and inconsistent state, showing why consistency is critical.
Consistency means the database enforces your business rules for you. You define the constraints once the DB ensures they are never violated by any transaction, ever.
Note: consistency in ACID is different from "consistency" in CAP theorem. ACID consistency means constraint validity. CAP consistency means all nodes see the same data at the same time.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 3. Isolation ( concurrent transactions don't interfere )

Multiple transactions running at the same time must behave as if they ran sequentially. One transaction's intermediate state must never be visible to another. Isolation is the most complex of the four properties and the one with the most trade-offs.
Without isolation: Two users both buy the last seat on a flight simultaneously. Both read stock=1, both decrement to 0, both get a ticket. The seat is now double-booked.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130293-311016006.png
With Isolation :
Here, transactions are handled one at a time in a controlled way. When User1 reads the available seat (1), the system locks it, so no other user can access it simultaneously.

User1 successfully books the seat, reducing it to 0. When User2 tries to read, they see 0 seats available, so the booking is denied. Each transaction is isolated, so no interference happens, and the system behaves correctly.
Without Isolation :
Here, multiple users access the data at the same time without any control. Both User1 and User2 read that 1 seat is available. Since there’s no isolation, both proceed to book it.
This results in double booking, where the system allows more bookings than available seats. This shows how lack of isolation leads to race conditions and incorrect data.
Isolation levels how strictly to enforce it
blocks.text: Isolation levels how strictly to enforce it

blocks.content: Perfect isolation has a performance cost. Databases offer levels you pick how much isolation you need for each transaction.

["Read Uncommitted (Lowest):
"]

["Read Committed (Low):
"]
However, if you read the same row twice in one transaction, you might get different values because another transaction could have updated it in between (non-repeatable read).

["Repeatable Read (High):
"]
This ensures stable reads. But if you query a range (like “all users with salary > 50k”), new rows inserted by other transactions can still appear (phantom reads).

["Serializable (Strongest):
"]
The downside is performance, as it requires heavy locking or conflict checks, so it’s used only when strict correctness is required.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024008-829810377.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of the four transaction isolation levels ordered from weakest to strongest: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable

blocks.content: 4. Durability ( committed means permanent )
Once a transaction is committed, the data is permanently saved even if the server crashes, loses power, or the process is killed the next millisecond. Committed data survives disasters.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130293-222034527.png
With Durability:
Once a transaction is committed, the data is permanently saved.
In the flow, payment succeeds → data is written → commit happens → even if the system crashes after that, the data is still (safe).
This is because databases store committed data on disk (using logs, replication, etc.). So no matter what happens after commit, the data will not be lost.
Without Durability:
Here, even though the payment is successful and data is written, it is not safely persisted. If the system crashes before the data is fully saved, everything is lost.
This means the system forgets that the payment ever happened, leading to serious issues like lost transactions or inconsistent state.
How Durability Actually Works (Step by Step)
blocks.text: How Durability Actually Works (Step by Step)

blocks.content: 1. Transaction executes (in memory)
When you run a query, the database first processes it in memory. This is fast, but memory is volatile if the system crashes now, everything is lost.
2. Write to WAL (Write-Ahead Log)
Before committing, the database writes all changes to a special log file on disk called the WAL.
This is done as a sequential write, which is very fast compared to random disk writes.
3. fsync → force write to disk
The database calls fsync() to ensure the WAL is physically written to disk (not just sitting in OS cache).
This is the critical durability moment once this step is done, data is safe.
4. COMMIT sent to client

Only after the WAL is safely stored on disk does the database respond:
“Transaction committed”
Now you can trust that your data won’t be lost.
5. Crash recovery (WAL replay)
If the system crashes after commit, on restart the database reads the WAL and replays all committed transactions.
This restores the database to the correct state automatically.

Durability has a cost every commit waits for anfsync()call. If you're writing 10,000 transactions/second, that's 10,000 disk flushes. This is why write throughput in SQL databases is bounded and why write-heavy systems reach for NoSQL.
5. All four working together ( one real transaction )
blocks.text: 5. All four working together ( one real transaction )

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282731955-708381351.png
blocks.alt: Sequence diagram of a UPI payment transaction from Arjun to Priya showing atomicity, isolation, consistency, and durability all applied together

blocks.content: A UPI payment from Arjun to Priya shows all four properties in action simultaneously.

BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- Isolation: other txns can't see our intermediate state

-- Step 1: debit Arjun
UPDATE accounts
  SET   balance = balance - 2000
  WHERE id = 'arjun'
    AND balance >= 2000;   -- Consistency: can't go negative

IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0
  ROLLBACK;               -- Atomicity: not enough balance → undo
  RETURN;
END IF;

-- Step 2: credit Priya
UPDATE accounts
  SET   balance = balance + 2000
  WHERE id = 'priya';

-- Step 3: record the transfer
INSERT INTO transactions
  (from_id, to_id, amount, timestamp)
  VALUES ('arjun', 'priya', 2000, NOW());

COMMIT;
-- Durability: fsynced to WAL. Permanent.
-- Atomicity: all 3 steps committed together.
-- Consistency: constraints satisfied.
-- Isolation: no other txn interfered.

items: Isolation (Serializable): Transaction runs as if it’s the only oneNo other transaction can see partial updates or interfere
Step 1: Debit Arjun (Consistency check) Deduct ₹2000 only if balance ≥ 2000Prevents negative balance (rule enforced)
Atomicity (failure handling): If debit fails (no balance), ROLLBACK happensEntire transaction is cancelled (nothing changes)
Step 2: Credit Priya ₹2000 is added to Priya’s account
Step 3: Record transaction Entry is stored in transactions tableKeeps history of the transfer
Durability: Data is written to disk (WAL + fsync)Even if system crashes, data is safe
Final result: All steps succeed together OR none happenDatabase remains correct and consistent.
